tools.name: configuration_view

tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Provides comprehensive metrics including CPU, memory, filesystem, and network usage at the node, pod, and container levels. On systems with cgroup v2 and kernel 4.20+, also includes PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics that show resource pressure for CPU, memory, and I/O. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/ for details on PSI metrics

name.description: Name of the node to get stats from

tools.name: nodes_top

name.description: Name of the Node to get the resource consumption from (Optional, all Nodes if not provided)

Here’s what I’ve done:

- Created the canary Deployment engine-v2-1 in canary-deployment-ns with 2 replicas using image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29, matching the stable deployment’s container name, containerPort (80), and security configuration.
- Updated the Service recommendation-engine to select app=recommendation-engine (removed the version filter) so it targets both the stable (v2.0) and canary (v2.1) pods. Kept port 80 -> targetPort 8080 unchanged.
- Result: With 2 replicas in engine-v2-0 and 2 replicas in engine-v2-1, the Service will distribute traffic across 4 endpoints, giving an approximate 50/50 split.

Current canary pods (Ready):
- engine-v2-1-7994887c57-w8dnq
- engine-v2-1-7994887c57-zfhdk

Notes and next steps:
- Adjust the split by scaling replicas (e.g., 3 stable / 1 canary ≈ 75/25).
- To roll back to stable-only traffic, set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0.
- Service-level load balancing is approximate; for precise weights consider an Ingress/Gateway with canary/weighting support.

- Change applied: Updated the Deployment to start nginx in the foreground:
  - command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
  - args: ["exec nginx -g 'daemon off;'"]
- Result: A new ReplicaSet rolled out and the pod is healthy:
  - Pod: app-84f6bf6c5c-vhgk7
  - Status: Running (1/1), Restarts: 0

Note: Alternatively, you can omit command/args entirely and rely on the nginx-unprivileged image’s default entrypoint.

results.taskOutput:
Summary
- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc requested storageClass "sc", which does not exist in the cluster. Events showed “storageclass.storage.k8s.io 'sc' not found.”
- Fix applied: I deleted the Pending PVC and recreated it to use the existing default StorageClass "standard".
- Result: The PVC is now Bound and the pod homepage-pod is Running (1/1) in namespace homepage-ns.

Details
- Available StorageClasses: standard (default), csi-hostpath-sc
- PVC status: homepage-pvc → Bound (1Gi) via StorageClass "standard"
- Pod status: homepage-pod → Running (1/1), Restarts: 0

Notes
- Changing storageClassName on an existing PVC is immutable, so recreation was required. Since the PVC hadn’t bound to any volume yet, no data was lost.
- If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or want to omit storageClassName to use the cluster default, I can update it accordingly.

pod/homepage-pod created

Summary
- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc requested storageClass "sc", which does not exist in the cluster. Events showed “storageclass.storage.k8s.io 'sc' not found.”
- Fix applied: I deleted the Pending PVC and recreated it to use the existing default StorageClass "standard".
- Result: The PVC is now Bound and the pod homepage-pod is Running (1/1) in namespace homepage-ns.

Details
- Available StorageClasses: standard (default), csi-hostpath-sc
- PVC status: homepage-pvc → Bound (1Gi) via StorageClass "standard"
- Pod status: homepage-pod → Running (1/1), Restarts: 0

Notes
- Changing storageClassName on an existing PVC is immutable, so recreation was required. Since the PVC hadn’t bound to any volume yet, no data was lost.
- If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or want to omit storageClassName to use the cluster default, I can update it accordingly.

outputSteps.content:
Summary
- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc requested storageClass "sc", which does not exist in the cluster. Events showed “storageclass.storage.k8s.io 'sc' not found.”
- Fix applied: I deleted the Pending PVC and recreated it to use the existing default StorageClass "standard".
- Result: The PVC is now Bound and the pod homepage-pod is Running (1/1) in namespace homepage-ns.

Details
- Available StorageClasses: standard (default), csi-hostpath-sc
- PVC status: homepage-pvc → Bound (1Gi) via StorageClass "standard"
- Pod status: homepage-pod → Running (1/1), Restarts: 0

Notes
- Changing storageClassName on an existing PVC is immutable, so recreation was required. Since the PVC hadn’t bound to any volume yet, no data was lost.
- If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or want to omit storageClassName to use the cluster default, I can update it accordingly.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (non-root cannot bind to 80), but:
  - The Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes were checking HTTP on port 80 at /get_status and /is_ready (paths that don’t exist).
  - The Service was targeting port 80, so even once up, traffic wouldn’t reach the container.

What I changed
- Updated the Service webapp (orders) to targetPort: 8080 (Service still exposes port 80 inside the cluster).
- Updated the Deployment webapp:
  - Probes now check GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposes container port 8080 (left 80 listed too; harmless, but I can remove it if you want).

Current status
- Deployment is healthy: 1/1 Ready and Available.
- Service endpoints are ready and point to the pod on port 8080.
- You can reach it inside the cluster at http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ (port 80 via Service).

Need external access?
- I can create an Ingress or a NodePort/LoadBalancer Service. Tell me your preferred hostname or exposure method.

namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (non-root cannot bind to 80), but:
  - The Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes were checking HTTP on port 80 at /get_status and /is_ready (paths that don’t exist).
  - The Service was targeting port 80, so even once up, traffic wouldn’t reach the container.

What I changed
- Updated the Service webapp (orders) to targetPort: 8080 (Service still exposes port 80 inside the cluster).
- Updated the Deployment webapp:
  - Probes now check GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposes container port 8080 (left 80 listed too; harmless, but I can remove it if you want).

Current status
- Deployment is healthy: 1/1 Ready and Available.
- Service endpoints are ready and point to the pod on port 8080.
- You can reach it inside the cluster at http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ (port 80 via Service).

Need external access?
- I can create an Ingress or a NodePort/LoadBalancer Service. Tell me your preferred hostname or exposure method.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service web/nginx was selecting app=web.
  - The Deployment labels Pods with app=nginx.
  - Result: no endpoints behind the Service, so it wasn’t routing to any Pod.
- The container listens on port 8080:
  - Inside the Pod, NGINX is configured to listen on 8080.
  - The Service’s targetPort was 80.
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic would have gone to the wrong port.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated Service web/nginx:
  - Selector: app=nginx (to match the Deployment’s Pod labels).
  - Port mapping: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (to match NGINX’s listen port).
- Verified:
  - Endpoints now show the Pod IP on port 8080.
  - From a test Pod in namespace web, HTTP GET to http://nginx returned 200 OK.
  - Cleaned up the temporary test Pods.

Current status
- web/nginx (ClusterIP) is reachable inside the cluster and returns HTTP 200.

Notes and next steps (if you need access from outside the cluster)
- The Service type is ClusterIP, so it’s only accessible within the cluster.
- If you want external access, choose one:
  - NodePort (exposes on every node’s IP at a high port).
  - LoadBalancer (cloud LB assigns an external IP).
  - Ingress (preferred for HTTP/HTTPS with hostname/TLS).
- Tell me your preference (and hostname/TLS details if using Ingress), and I’ll set it up.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service web/nginx was selecting app=web.
  - The Deployment labels Pods with app=nginx.
  - Result: no endpoints behind the Service, so it wasn’t routing to any Pod.
- The container listens on port 8080:
  - Inside the Pod, NGINX is configured to listen on 8080.
  - The Service’s targetPort was 80.
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic would have gone to the wrong port.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated Service web/nginx:
  - Selector: app=nginx (to match the Deployment’s Pod labels).
  - Port mapping: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (to match NGINX’s listen port).
- Verified:
  - Endpoints now show the Pod IP on port 8080.
  - From a test Pod in namespace web, HTTP GET to http://nginx returned 200 OK.
  - Cleaned up the temporary test Pods.

Current status
- web/nginx (ClusterIP) is reachable inside the cluster and returns HTTP 200.

Notes and next steps (if you need access from outside the cluster)
- The Service type is ClusterIP, so it’s only accessible within the cluster.
- If you want external access, choose one:
  - NodePort (exposes on every node’s IP at a high port).
  - LoadBalancer (cloud LB assigns an external IP).
  - Ingress (preferred for HTTP/HTTPS with hostname/TLS).
- Tell me your preference (and hostname/TLS details if using Ingress), and I’ll set it up.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service web/nginx was selecting app=web.
  - The Deployment labels Pods with app=nginx.
  - Result: no endpoints behind the Service, so it wasn’t routing to any Pod.
- The container listens on port 8080:
  - Inside the Pod, NGINX is configured to listen on 8080.
  - The Service’s targetPort was 80.
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic would have gone to the wrong port.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated Service web/nginx:
  - Selector: app=nginx (to match the Deployment’s Pod labels).
  - Port mapping: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (to match NGINX’s listen port).
- Verified:
  - Endpoints now show the Pod IP on port 8080.
  - From a test Pod in namespace web, HTTP GET to http://nginx returned 200 OK.
  - Cleaned up the temporary test Pods.

Current status
- web/nginx (ClusterIP) is reachable inside the cluster and returns HTTP 200.

Notes and next steps (if you need access from outside the cluster)
- The Service type is ClusterIP, so it’s only accessible within the cluster.
- If you want external access, choose one:
  - NodePort (exposes on every node’s IP at a high port).
  - LoadBalancer (cloud LB assigns an external IP).
  - Ingress (preferred for HTTP/HTTPS with hostname/TLS).
- Tell me your preference (and hostname/TLS details if using Ingress), and I’ll set it up.

results.taskOutput:
Thanks for the details. I found and fixed two separate issues that caused your frontend pods not to run and the “connection refused” errors.

What was wrong
- Scheduling constraint blocked pods
  - The Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu.
  - Your cluster’s only node doesn’t have that label, so the pods stayed Pending with FailedScheduling.
- Service pointed to the wrong port
  - The nginx-unprivileged image is listening on port 8080 (nginx default in that image).
  - The Service web-app-service was targeting port 80, so connections to the Service were forwarded to container port 80 where nothing was listening, causing connection refused.

What I changed
- Deployment: removed the nodeSelector so the pods can schedule on the available node.
  - Resource: apps/v1 Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment
- Service: updated targetPort to 8080 to match the container.
  - Resource: v1 Service webshop-frontend/web-app-service

Current status (post-fix)
- Pods are running:
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-g8bgg Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-dw5nq Running
- Service now selects the pods and targets container port 8080. Endpoints are populated for the two pods.

How to verify
- Inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -o wide
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get svc web-app-service -o yaml | grep -A2 targetPort
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
  - Quick curl test:
    - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run tmp-curl --rm -it --image=alpine/curl -- sh -lc 'curl -sI http://web-app-service/'
- From a workstation (optional):
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend port-forward svc/web-app-service 8080:80
  - curl -sI http://localhost:8080/

Recommendations to prevent recurrence
- Align ports explicitly:
  - In the Deployment, set containerPort: 8080 (not strictly required but avoids confusion).
  - In the Service, keep targetPort: 8080 (or use a named port in the pod spec and reference that name in the Service).
- Probes:
  - Add a readinessProbe (HTTP GET / on port 8080) so Endpoints are only added when nginx is ready.
- Scheduling intent:
  - If you really need GPU/production nodes later, either label the nodes appropriately or use nodeAffinity/tolerations; otherwise keep nodeSelector unset.

I also cleaned up the short-lived test pods used for verification. Let me know if you want me to add readiness/liveness probes and port naming to the Deployment manifest.

namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created

Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Thanks for the details. I found and fixed two separate issues that caused your frontend pods not to run and the “connection refused” errors.

What was wrong
- Scheduling constraint blocked pods
  - The Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu.
  - Your cluster’s only node doesn’t have that label, so the pods stayed Pending with FailedScheduling.
- Service pointed to the wrong port
  - The nginx-unprivileged image is listening on port 8080 (nginx default in that image).
  - The Service web-app-service was targeting port 80, so connections to the Service were forwarded to container port 80 where nothing was listening, causing connection refused.

What I changed
- Deployment: removed the nodeSelector so the pods can schedule on the available node.
  - Resource: apps/v1 Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment
- Service: updated targetPort to 8080 to match the container.
  - Resource: v1 Service webshop-frontend/web-app-service

Current status (post-fix)
- Pods are running:
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-g8bgg Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-dw5nq Running
- Service now selects the pods and targets container port 8080. Endpoints are populated for the two pods.

How to verify
- Inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -o wide
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get svc web-app-service -o yaml | grep -A2 targetPort
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
  - Quick curl test:
    - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run tmp-curl --rm -it --image=alpine/curl -- sh -lc 'curl -sI http://web-app-service/'
- From a workstation (optional):
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend port-forward svc/web-app-service 8080:80
  - curl -sI http://localhost:8080/

Recommendations to prevent recurrence
- Align ports explicitly:
  - In the Deployment, set containerPort: 8080 (not strictly required but avoids confusion).
  - In the Service, keep targetPort: 8080 (or use a named port in the pod spec and reference that name in the Service).
- Probes:
  - Add a readinessProbe (HTTP GET / on port 8080) so Endpoints are only added when nginx is ready.
- Scheduling intent:
  - If you really need GPU/production nodes later, either label the nodes appropriately or use nodeAffinity/tolerations; otherwise keep nodeSelector unset.

I also cleaned up the short-lived test pods used for verification. Let me know if you want me to add readiness/liveness probes and port naming to the Deployment manifest.

outputSteps.content:
Thanks for the details. I found and fixed two separate issues that caused your frontend pods not to run and the “connection refused” errors.

What was wrong
- Scheduling constraint blocked pods
  - The Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu.
  - Your cluster’s only node doesn’t have that label, so the pods stayed Pending with FailedScheduling.
- Service pointed to the wrong port
  - The nginx-unprivileged image is listening on port 8080 (nginx default in that image).
  - The Service web-app-service was targeting port 80, so connections to the Service were forwarded to container port 80 where nothing was listening, causing connection refused.

What I changed
- Deployment: removed the nodeSelector so the pods can schedule on the available node.
  - Resource: apps/v1 Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment
- Service: updated targetPort to 8080 to match the container.
  - Resource: v1 Service webshop-frontend/web-app-service

Current status (post-fix)
- Pods are running:
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-g8bgg Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-dw5nq Running
- Service now selects the pods and targets container port 8080. Endpoints are populated for the two pods.

How to verify
- Inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -o wide
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get svc web-app-service -o yaml | grep -A2 targetPort
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
  - Quick curl test:
    - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run tmp-curl --rm -it --image=alpine/curl -- sh -lc 'curl -sI http://web-app-service/'
- From a workstation (optional):
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend port-forward svc/web-app-service 8080:80
  - curl -sI http://localhost:8080/

Recommendations to prevent recurrence
- Align ports explicitly:
  - In the Deployment, set containerPort: 8080 (not strictly required but avoids confusion).
  - In the Service, keep targetPort: 8080 (or use a named port in the pod spec and reference that name in the Service).
- Probes:
  - Add a readinessProbe (HTTP GET / on port 8080) so Endpoints are only added when nginx is ready.
- Scheduling intent:
  - If you really need GPU/production nodes later, either label the nodes appropriately or use nodeAffinity/tolerations; otherwise keep nodeSelector unset.

I also cleaned up the short-lived test pods used for verification. Let me know if you want me to add readiness/liveness probes and port naming to the Deployment manifest.

Here’s what I found for the control-plane (master) nodes’ resource usage.

Notes:

- The cluster has 1 control-plane node: mcp-eval-cluster.

Node mcp-eval-cluster (capacity: 4 vCPU, 15.6 GiB RAM, 144.2 GiB disk)
- CPU: ~0.084 cores in use now (~2.1% of 4 vCPU)
- Memory: ~3.66 GiB used (~23.5% of 15.6 GiB); working set ~1.26 GiB (~8.1%)
- Filesystem: ~67.4 GiB used of 144.2 GiB (~46.8% used); imagefs used ~3.1 GiB
- Swap: ~0.33 MiB used of ~3.0 GiB (near zero)
- PIDs: 631 in use of max 127,591 (<<1%)

Key control-plane pods on the node (approximate instant usage)
- kube-apiserver: ~0.024 cores; ~426 MiB RSS/WS
- etcd: ~0.020 cores; ~67 MiB WS
- kube-controller-manager: ~0.008 cores; ~69 MiB WS

If you want kubectl top to work, I can install Metrics Server for ongoing “top” style CPU/memory reporting.

Done.

What I changed:
- Increased the PVC used by the pod:
  - PVC: resize-pv/storage-pvc
  - StorageClass: csi-hostpath-sc (supports expansion)
  - Requested size updated from 1Gi to 3Gi
- The underlying PV now has capacity 3Gi.
- Restarted storage-pod to complete the filesystem resize.
- storage-pod is back to Running.

Quick verification commands:
- PVC capacity:
  - kubectl -n resize-pv get pvc storage-pvc -o jsonpath='{.status.capacity.storage}'; echo
- Inside the pod (should show ~3G on the mount):
  - kubectl -n resize-pv exec -it storage-pod -- sh -lc 'df -h /usr/share/nginx/html'

If you want me to double-check the filesystem size from inside the pod now, I can run the commands and report back.

results.taskOutput:
All set. I created the requested namespaces, RBAC, resource quotas, and network policies to provide a secure, multi-tenant dev environment for alice, bob, and charlie, following least-privilege and strong isolation.

What’s configured

1) Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared
- staging, prod

2) RBAC
- Each developer has full developer-level access to their own namespace via RoleBinding to ClusterRole edit:
  - dev-alice: subjects alice and SA dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob: subjects bob and SA dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: subjects charlie and SA dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Read-only access to dev-shared for all developers and their service accounts via RoleBinding to ClusterRole view (subjects: users alice, bob, charlie; SAs dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa)
- Staging and prod: no developer bindings created. Only cluster-admins retain access by existing cluster-admin bindings.
- ServiceAccounts created:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa

Note: I bound developers to ClusterRole edit (not admin) to honor least privilege while still granting full development capabilities in their namespaces (CRUD on most resources, logs/exec). If you explicitly want namespace-level RBAC administration by developers, I can swap to admin.

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu: 2
  - limits.memory: 4Gi
  - pods: 10
  - services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu: 4
  - limits.memory: 8Gi
  - pods: 20
  - services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu: 8
  - limits.memory: 16Gi
  - pods: 50
  - services: 20

4) Network Policies
- Default deny for ingress and egress in all six namespaces (baseline isolation).
- Allow DNS egress (UDP/TCP 53) to kube-system in all six namespaces (so pods can resolve names).
- Allow same-namespace traffic (ingress and egress) in each namespace.
- Dev namespace to dev-shared:
  - In dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: allow egress to namespace dev-shared only.
  - In dev-shared: allow ingress from dev namespaces (specifically from namespaces labeled environment=dev and tenant in [alice, bob, charlie]).
- Cross-developer isolation: no policies permit dev-namespace-to-dev-namespace traffic; only same-namespace and dev-shared are allowed.
- Staging/prod isolation: only same-namespace traffic is allowed; nothing from dev namespaces is allowed in or out.

5) Principle of least privilege and isolation
- Developers have no RBAC in staging/prod and cannot reach those namespaces over the network.
- Dev namespaces cannot talk to each other; they can only talk to dev-shared and DNS.
- System namespaces are not changed; default deny policies are applied only to your six dev/stage/prod namespaces.

How to verify (quick checks)

RBAC
- kubectl auth can-i --as alice -n dev-alice create deploy
- kubectl auth can-i --as alice -n dev-bob get pods            # expect: no
- kubectl auth can-i --as alice -n dev-shared get pods         # expect: yes
- kubectl auth can-i --as alice -n dev-shared delete pods      # expect: no
- kubectl auth can-i --as alice -n staging get pods            # expect: no
- kubectl auth can-i --as alice -n prod get pods               # expect: no

Quotas
- kubectl -n dev-alice describe resourcequota rq-standard
- kubectl -n dev-shared describe resourcequota rq-shared
- kubectl -n staging describe resourcequota rq-staging
- kubectl -n prod describe resourcequota rq-prod

Network policies (functional probes)
- From a pod in dev-alice:
  - Access a pod/service in dev-alice: should succeed
  - Access a pod/service in dev-bob: should be blocked
  - Access a pod/service in dev-shared: should succeed
  - nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local: should succeed (DNS allowed)

Notes and options
- User identities alice, bob, charlie must be provided by your cluster’s auth (e.g., OIDC or client cert CN). If their usernames differ in the IdP, update the RoleBinding subjects accordingly.
- If you want developers to manage namespace RBAC (Roles/RoleBindings) themselves, switch RoleBindings from edit to admin. By default we used edit to avoid RBAC escalation.
- If your workloads need additional “system services” beyond DNS (for example, direct access to the Kubernetes API via kubernetes.default.svc:443), we can add narrowly-scoped egress rules for that target.

If you want, I can export all applied resources into a single YAML bundle for GitOps.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All set. I created the requested namespaces, RBAC, resource quotas, and network policies to provide a secure, multi-tenant dev environment for alice, bob, and charlie, following least-privilege and strong isolation.

What’s configured

1) Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared
- staging, prod

2) RBAC
- Each developer has full developer-level access to their own namespace via RoleBinding to ClusterRole edit:
  - dev-alice: subjects alice and SA dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob: subjects bob and SA dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: subjects charlie and SA dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Read-only access to dev-shared for all developers and their service accounts via RoleBinding to ClusterRole view (subjects: users alice, bob, charlie; SAs dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa)
- Staging and prod: no developer bindings created. Only cluster-admins retain access by existing cluster-admin bindings.
- ServiceAccounts created:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa

Note: I bound developers to ClusterRole edit (not admin) to honor least privilege while still granting full development capabilities in their namespaces (CRUD on most resources, logs/exec). If you explicitly want namespace-level RBAC administration by developers, I can swap to admin.

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu: 2
  - limits.memory: 4Gi
  - pods: 10
  - services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu: 4
  - limits.memory: 8Gi
  - pods: 20
  - services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu: 8
  - limits.memory: 16Gi
  - pods: 50
  - services: 20

4) Network Policies
- Default deny for ingress and egress in all six namespaces (baseline isolation).
- Allow DNS egress (UDP/TCP 53) to kube-system in all six namespaces (so pods can resolve names).
- Allow same-namespace traffic (ingress and egress) in each namespace.
- Dev namespace to dev-shared:
  - In dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: allow egress to namespace dev-shared only.
  - In dev-shared: allow ingress from dev namespaces (specifically from namespaces labeled environment=dev and tenant in [alice, bob, charlie]).
- Cross-developer isolation: no policies permit dev-namespace-to-dev-namespace traffic; only same-namespace and dev-shared are allowed.
- Staging/prod isolation: only same-namespace traffic is allowed; nothing from dev namespaces is allowed in or out.

5) Principle of least privilege and isolation
- Developers have no RBAC in staging/prod and cannot reach those namespaces over the network.
- Dev namespaces cannot talk to each other; they can only talk to dev-shared and DNS.
- System namespaces are not changed; default deny policies are applied only to your six dev/stage/prod namespaces.

How to verify (quick checks)

RBAC
- kubectl auth can-i --as alice -n dev-alice create deploy
- kubectl auth can-i --as alice -n dev-bob get pods            # expect: no
- kubectl auth can-i --as alice -n dev-shared get pods         # expect: yes
- kubectl auth can-i --as alice -n dev-shared delete pods      # expect: no
- kubectl auth can-i --as alice -n staging get pods            # expect: no
- kubectl auth can-i --as alice -n prod get pods               # expect: no

Quotas
- kubectl -n dev-alice describe resourcequota rq-standard
- kubectl -n dev-shared describe resourcequota rq-shared
- kubectl -n staging describe resourcequota rq-staging
- kubectl -n prod describe resourcequota rq-prod

Network policies (functional probes)
- From a pod in dev-alice:
  - Access a pod/service in dev-alice: should succeed
  - Access a pod/service in dev-bob: should be blocked
  - Access a pod/service in dev-shared: should succeed
  - nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local: should succeed (DNS allowed)

Notes and options
- User identities alice, bob, charlie must be provided by your cluster’s auth (e.g., OIDC or client cert CN). If their usernames differ in the IdP, update the RoleBinding subjects accordingly.
- If you want developers to manage namespace RBAC (Roles/RoleBindings) themselves, switch RoleBindings from edit to admin. By default we used edit to avoid RBAC escalation.
- If your workloads need additional “system services” beyond DNS (for example, direct access to the Kubernetes API via kubernetes.default.svc:443), we can add narrowly-scoped egress rules for that target.

If you want, I can export all applied resources into a single YAML bundle for GitOps.

Note: I bound developers to ClusterRole edit (not admin) to honor least privilege while still granting full development capabilities in their namespaces (CRUD on most resources, logs/exec). If you explicitly want namespace-level RBAC administration by developers, I can swap to admin.

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu: 2
  - limits.memory: 4Gi
  - pods: 10
  - services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu: 4
  - limits.memory: 8Gi
  - pods: 20
  - services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu: 8
  - limits.memory: 16Gi
  - pods: 50
  - services: 20

4) Network Policies
- Default deny for ingress and egress in all six namespaces (baseline isolation).
- Allow DNS egress (UDP/TCP 53) to kube-system in all six namespaces (so pods can resolve names).
- Allow same-namespace traffic (ingress and egress) in each namespace.
- Dev namespace to dev-shared:
  - In dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: allow egress to namespace dev-shared only.
  - In dev-shared: allow ingress from dev namespaces (specifically from namespaces labeled environment=dev and tenant in [alice, bob, charlie]).
- Cross-developer isolation: no policies permit dev-namespace-to-dev-namespace traffic; only same-namespace and dev-shared are allowed.
- Staging/prod isolation: only same-namespace traffic is allowed; nothing from dev namespaces is allowed in or out.

5) Principle of least privilege and isolation
- Developers have no RBAC in staging/prod and cannot reach those namespaces over the network.
- Dev namespaces cannot talk to each other; they can only talk to dev-shared and DNS.
- System namespaces are not changed; default deny policies are applied only to your six dev/stage/prod namespaces.

How to verify (quick checks)

RBAC
- kubectl auth can-i --as alice -n dev-alice create deploy
- kubectl auth can-i --as alice -n dev-bob get pods            # expect: no
- kubectl auth can-i --as alice -n dev-shared get pods         # expect: yes
- kubectl auth can-i --as alice -n dev-shared delete pods      # expect: no
- kubectl auth can-i --as alice -n staging get pods            # expect: no
- kubectl auth can-i --as alice -n prod get pods               # expect: no

Quotas
- kubectl -n dev-alice describe resourcequota rq-standard
- kubectl -n dev-shared describe resourcequota rq-shared
- kubectl -n staging describe resourcequota rq-staging
- kubectl -n prod describe resourcequota rq-prod

Network policies (functional probes)
- From a pod in dev-alice:
  - Access a pod/service in dev-alice: should succeed
  - Access a pod/service in dev-bob: should be blocked
  - Access a pod/service in dev-shared: should succeed
  - nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local: should succeed (DNS allowed)

Notes and options
- User identities alice, bob, charlie must be provided by your cluster’s auth (e.g., OIDC or client cert CN). If their usernames differ in the IdP, update the RoleBinding subjects accordingly.
- If you want developers to manage namespace RBAC (Roles/RoleBindings) themselves, switch RoleBindings from edit to admin. By default we used edit to avoid RBAC escalation.
- If your workloads need additional “system services” beyond DNS (for example, direct access to the Kubernetes API via kubernetes.default.svc:443), we can add narrowly-scoped egress rules for that target.

If you want, I can export all applied resources into a single YAML bundle for GitOps.

outputSteps.content:
Summary diagnosis
- Immediate failure reason: CouldntGetTask — the PipelineRun references a Task named missing-task that doesn’t exist or can’t be resolved.
- Evidence:
  - PipelineRun tekton-eval/failed-run status: "Couldn't retrieve Task 'missing-task': tasks.tekton.dev 'missing-task' not found"
  - Events show Failed/InternalError with the same message.
  - A TaskRun was created (failed-run-missing-pipeline) but Succeeded=False with Reason=TaskRunResolutionFailed; no pod was ever started.
  - No pods for this PipelineRun were created.

What this means
- The Pipeline broken-pipeline includes a taskRef to a Task named missing-task:
  - status.pipelineSpec.tasks[0].taskRef.name = missing-task
- Because taskRef is just name/kind=Task (no resolver/bundle), Tekton expects a namespaced Task named missing-task in tekton-eval. It isn’t there.

Pipeline-as-Code (PaC) and TektonConfig context
- Pipelines-as-Code Repository CRDs were not found (no matches for pipelinesascode.tekton.dev Repository v1alpha1/v1beta1). This suggests PaC isn’t installed or used in this cluster/namespace. There is no Repository object to tie this run to.
- TektonConfig CRD from the Tekton Operator was not found (no matches for operator.tekton.dev TektonConfig). Tekton may have been installed without the Operator (or with different CRDs). This isn’t the cause of the failure but explains why there’s no cluster-wide TektonConfig to inspect.

Most likely root cause
- The Task missing-task is absent from the tekton-eval namespace, and no alternative resolution (ClusterTask, bundle, or resolver like git/hub) is specified.

Recommended next actions
1) Decide how you intend to provide the task and fix the reference:
   - Namespaced Task: create the Task named missing-task in tekton-eval.
     - kubectl apply -n tekton-eval -f task-missing-task.yaml
     - or install from Tekton Hub if applicable: tkn hub install task missing-task -n tekton-eval
   - Cluster-scoped Task: if it’s a ClusterTask, change taskRef.kind to ClusterTask and ensure that ClusterTask missing-task exists.
   - Remote/bundled Task: if you meant to resolve from git/hub/bundle, update taskRef to use a resolver or bundle and ensure the resolver is installed and configured. Examples:
     - taskRef:
         resolver: git
         params: [{name: url, value: ...}, {name: pathInRepo, value: task.yaml}, {name: revision, value: ...}]
     - taskRef:
         resolver: hub
         params: [{name: name, value: missing-task}, {name: version, value: ...}]
     - taskRef:
         bundle: registry.example.com/mybundle:tag
         name: missing-task
   - Inline the Task in the Pipeline as taskSpec if that suits your workflow.

2) Re-run after the fix:
   - Create a new PipelineRun or restart this one. If you want, I can restart failed-run once the Task/reference is corrected.

Optional quick checks
- Verify presence of the Task now: kubectl get task missing-task -n tekton-eval
- List installed tasks: kubectl get task -n tekton-eval
- If you expect PaC, install/configure pipelines-as-code and create a Repository resource in tekton-eval.

If you share how you want to source missing-task (local YAML, ClusterTask, Hub, git, or bundle), I can provide an exact manifest update or apply it and then restart the run.
